content.title: Artemis II latest: 'It was a very intense 13 minutes' - Moon mission astronauts describe what it was like falling back to Earth
content.text: That's all for now We're wrapping up our live coverage of the Artemis II space mission for today.The crew spoke at their first news conference this evening since returning to Earth.They discussed some of the highs of the trip, moments that stuck with them and about broken toilets.Scroll down to catch up in full, but here's some of what was said:A movie couldn't do the mission "justice", pilot Victor Glover said - he suggested a TV series would be more appropriate;Commander Reid Wiseman admitted that if they'd had a lander, the crew might've tried to land on the moon as they got so close;He also defended the ship's toilet, which had intermittent issues, as a "wonderful toilet" and told the engineers behind it to hold their heads "very high";The crew offered their advice to any youngsters now looking to the stars, inspired by their flight;While during calls with families back on Earth, all of the astronauts cried, one admitted;Christina Koch said she'd struggled with the lack of zero gravity since returning to Earth and offered her advice to any female astronauts following her into space;Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen spoke of feeling "infinitesimally small, but yet very powerful as a human being, as a group" during the mission;And Wiseman said the four of them were "bonded forever" after their mission. Christina Koch's advice to any female astronauts following in her footsteps Christina Koch, one of the four crew members of the Artemis II mission, was the first woman to travel to the moon.In the final question of the news conference, she was asked what her advice would be to a female astronaut who would become the first to ever walk on the moon.Here's what she said:"For me, I think the biggest word about all of the superlatives that you're going to encounter, all of the things that you're going to be asked to do; react, to be a part of, contribute to - it's humbling. "And if you remember that being part of a team is your main goal, and the main thing that you put ahead of everything else, then when the world tries to make the accomplishment something different than what it really is, which is a team accomplishment, you will know, and the things that you say will reflect how you really see it."The news conference has now finished. 'A movie couldn't do it justice': Artemis crew on screen adaption Artemis pilot Victor Glover says a movie couldn't do their experience "justice" and a series would be needed to capture the scope of the journey.Astronaut Christina Koch adds that it would be hard to convey the feeling of how amazing it has been to inspire the support of the public. She says:"I guess the thing that might be hardest to convey, no matter what the platform would be, how much it meant to us to bring everyone along with us, and how much it meant to us to hear that the mission had an impact. "I cannot overstate how important that was to us. "It was every bit as important as accomplishing the technical goals, and being there for our NASA teammates was to make this the world's mission, and for it to have a positive impact on as much of the world as possible." 'The unknown is way scarier than the known' Astronaut Christina Koch is expressing confidence that a future Artemis mission will land on the moon.She says the mission taught her that it is possible to accomplish their goals with hard work.She says:"This mission taught me that the unknown is way scarier than the known. "Every single time we accomplished a mission test objective, we all looked at each other and we're like, 'that actually went pretty well'. "That was actually not necessarily easy, because it took a ton of work, but it was easy to accomplish as a team because we had put in the work. "We know how to put in the work to make it accomplish a goal when the time comes." 'If we had a lander we would've been down on the moon' Commander Reid Wiseman says he had one "weird technical epiphany" when out in space.That was how close they were to actually landing on the moon. He says:"I'm telling you right now, if we had a first flight lander on board that thing, I know at least three of my crewmates would have been in it trying to land on the moon."Wiseman says the mission was "not the leap I thought it was" - but admitted he might eat his own words.For the next crew up on the Artemis programme, he adds: "It's going to be extremely technically challenging, but this team needs to show up every day knowing it is absolutely doable. And it's doable soon." 'That was a wonderful toilet': Artemis commander defends toilet despite issues During their mission, the Artemis II crew had intermittent issues with their toilet.The problem centred around clogs in the wastewater pipes, preventing them from emptying.But Commander Reid Wiseman defended the toilet, and those who made it."I just want to say 100% point blank, that was a wonderful toilet. The toilet worked great, where we had an issue, and it was an issue for sure, is that our primary vent line when you go to the bathroom, you flush the toilet, the toilet flushes just fine. But then when the liquid went out the bottom of the toilet, it got clogged up in our vent line and our tank can only hold about, maybe like under 10 urination events."But Wiseman said for the first two days, he enjoyed watching the tank get dumped out into space."It's just like a billion little tiny flecks of ice heading up into deep space."Then he told the engineers behind the toilet to hold their heads "very high". 'Everyone who has a dream gets to work equally hard to achieve that dream' The Artemis crew is being asked if they support NASA's pledge to put the first woman and the first person of colour on the moon when the next landing takes place. A journalist claims that this promise has since been removed from NASA's website, and asked if the astronauts believed this promise should be kept. Astronaut Christina Koch says:"I do think that's something to celebrate, that decades ago, we made the decision that everyone who has a dream gets to work equally hard to achieve that dream."And that if we're not going for all and by all, we aren't answering humanity's call to explore, which is what we do here." 'Me space' is a myth during mission, Artemis crew say The astronauts from Artemis are joking that there isn't "much me time" in space.Artemis pilot Victor Glover reflects that "'me space' was maybe a myth" on Artemis, adding that when one person was exercising, they all did due to a lack of space. He says:"'Me space' was maybe a myth, that 15-minute checkout when you're talking to your family, it did feel like being teleported out of the vehicle, but you teleported right back. "And so, we embraced that. That was a part of it, though."He adds that good communication was key because the crew was "crawling all over each other for 10 days". "But we did get good at that too," he says. Artemis II crew give their advice to youngsters 'looking skywards now' The Artemis II crew are asked what advice they'd give to youngsters who are "looking skywards now".Reid Wiseman calls on young people to not be afraid of doing difficult things, adding "our hands and our minds have got to be engaged";Victor Glover says youngsters should "start now" asking questions but being very prepared to listen: "Yes it is my call sign, but I do not know everything" (his call sign is Ike - which stands for "I know everything");Christina Koch says: "Find what you can do the slowest the longest", as well as doing "what scares you" and not being afraid to meet resistance. But she also calls on youngsters to support those around you;Speaking last, Jeremy Hansen says: "Follow the example people saw here, don't do it alone...you need the support of others to do big things." 'Every one of us cried': Astronauts reflect on mementos from Earth Astronaut Reid Wiseman says he took notes with messages written by friends and a bracelet his daughter made into space with him.On the emotional weight of the items he brought, Wiseman says: "Things that were so important to you when you launch can be less important in space, and things that were just an afterthought in space can become the absolute most important thing that you possibly can possibly take. So I think overall, we did a pretty good job with that."He says each of them got two chances to call their families from space."Everyone of us cried. I mean, nobody didn't get through those things without crying," he says.
